subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.activity_title: What Is Data and Why Does It Matter?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates? (Open-ended process question on data organisation.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the most popular game in their class? (Read and interpret the raw data list to identify hockey as the most frequent.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pari wants to respond to four questions. Put a tick for questions requiring data collection and a cross for those that do not: (a) most popular TV show among classmates; (b) when India got independence; (c) water wasted in her locality; (d) capital of India.

time_bands.activity: Open discussion: the teacher writes several everyday questions on the board — 'Which sport do most students in our class like?' and 'What is the capital of India?' — and asks students which questions need collecting new information and which can be answered from memory. This surfaces the intuitive idea of data as collected facts.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75 ("What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates?...") and Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.75 ("What is the most popular game in their class?...") using the raw list in the textbook. Pairs discuss what makes the raw list hard to read and how they found the answer.

Class discussion of Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.75 ("Pari wants to respond to four questions. Put a tick for questions requiring data collection..."). Students justify each tick or cross aloud, reinforcing the distinction between look-up facts and collected data.

Teacher consolidates by naming the key vocabulary — data, raw data, frequency — and asking students to state in their own words what data is and give one example from daily life. A brief oral round closes the discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: The distinction between facts one already knows and facts one must collect is the conceptual anchor of this unit; watch for students who believe any answered question counts as 'data'. Figure it Out Q2 on p.75 works best after students have tried Q1, because experiencing the difficulty of the raw list makes the answer to 'what is the most popular game' genuinely hard to find.

periods.activity_title: Tally Marks, Frequency Tables, and Ordered Data

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh's sweet-preference data. Sub-parts: (a) students who chose jalebi; (b) barfi count; (c) gujiya count; (d) rasgulla count; (e) gulab jamun count.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the frequency table sufficient to distribute each type of sweet to the correct student? Explain. If not, what is the alternative?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Help Sushri Sandhya figure out from shoe-size data arranged in ascending order: (a) largest shoe size; (b) smallest shoe size; (c) number of students wearing size 5; (d) number wearing sizes larger than 4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: How did arranging the data in ascending order help answer the shoe-size questions?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.75
homework.description: Try to find out the most popular game among your own classmates. (Real data collection activity.)

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly models the tally-mark convention on the board — groups of five, the fifth as a diagonal — so every student has the notation before working independently.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76 ("Complete the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh's sweet-preference data...") individually, then compare answers with a neighbour. Teacher circulates and checks that tally groups of five are formed correctly.

Class discussion of Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 ("Is the frequency table sufficient to distribute each type of sweet to the correct student?..."). Students articulate why a frequency count alone cannot name who gets which sweet, surfacing the difference between aggregate and individual data.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.77 ("Help Sushri Sandhya figure out from shoe-size data arranged in ascending order..."), followed by the Math Talk in Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 ("How did arranging the data in ascending order help...?"). Pairs share responses aloud.

Teacher sets Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.75 ("Try to find out the most popular game among your own classmates...") as a take-home data-collection task, explaining what a tally sheet looks like so students can carry one home.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip is tallying in ones rather than in grouped fives — marking this explicitly when circulating prevents cascading errors in the frequency count. For the shoe-size discussion, watch for students who confuse ascending order with frequency order; the data is arranged by size value, not by how common a size is.

periods.activity_title: Data in the Wild: Trees, Newspapers, and Real Counts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: Are there other ways to arrange the shoe-size data?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write names of trees seen on the way from home to school, record observations, complete a frequency table, then answer: (a) tree found in greatest number; (b) tree in smallest number; (c) any two trees found in equal numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Paste a newspaper article, count letters c, e, i, r, x and one other of your choice, fill a frequency table. Sub-parts: (a) most frequent letter; (b) least frequent letter; (c) list the five letters in ascending frequency order and compare with classmates; (d) write the process followed; (e) discuss classmates' processes; (f) what process would you follow with a different article?

time_bands.activity: Quick Math Talk using Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.77 ("Are there other ways to arrange the shoe-size data?"). Students suggest descending order, grouping by size category, etc., and the class agrees that the key value of any arrangement is making comparisons easier.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.78 ("Write names of trees seen on the way from home to school..."). Since this is a home-observation task, the teacher asks students to recall trees from their walk to school today, estimate counts, construct a tally table on paper, and answer parts (a)–(c). Small groups compare their local tree lists.

Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.78 ("Paste a newspaper article, count letters c, e, i, r, x..."). Using a short printed or teacher-written passage on the board, the class tallies the five specified letters together, fills in the frequency table, and works through sub-parts (a)–(c). Each student then writes, in one sentence, the process they followed (sub-part d).
Pairs compare their process descriptions (sub-part e) and discuss: would they change their counting method for a longer article (sub-part f)? Two volunteers share their answers with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The letter-frequency task in Figure it Out Q5 (p.78) often reveals that students count letters by scanning randomly rather than line by line — drawing attention to systematic row-by-row counting is the key process insight. Students who finished the tree-observation homework from the previous unit may use their own data for Q4 instead of estimating.
materials: Blackboard with a short passage written on it or printed handout

periods.activity_title: Reading Pictographs: Symbols, Scales, and Half-Symbols

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.2 p.80
textbook_items_in_class.description: Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours. Students read the pictograph (each symbol = 10 children) to find: children who always slept ≥9 hours (50), sometimes (25), and never (40). Full solutions provided demonstrating how to handle full and half symbols.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 4.2 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: What problems would arise in preparing a pictograph (where one symbol = 10 students, half = 5) if the total number of students in a class is 33 or 27?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.2 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the pictograph of books borrowed from Middle School Ginnori library over a week to answer: (a) day with minimum books borrowed; (b) total books borrowed during the week; (c) day with maximum books borrowed and possible reason.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple pictograph on the board with five rows and a key of one smiley = 2 items, and asks: 'What does each symbol stand for? What does half a symbol mean?' Students identify the three essential parts of any pictograph — title, symbols, key — by pointing them out in the teacher's drawing.

Class works through Example, section 4.2 p.80 ("Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours...") together. Teacher reads one row aloud, students count symbols and apply the key (each symbol = 10 children). The half-symbol row is worked carefully: students state what half of 10 is before writing the answer.

Math Talk, section 4.2 p.83 ("What problems would arise in preparing a pictograph...if the total number of students is 33 or 27?"). Students reason in pairs: 33 cannot be expressed as a whole number of tens plus a half, so a symbol-equals-10 scale breaks down. Class shares conclusions.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 4.2 p.83 ("Use the pictograph of books borrowed from Middle School Ginnori library over a week...") individually, answering parts (a)–(c). Teacher takes oral answers and asks students to state which part of the key they used for each answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The concept that a pictograph's key is mandatory — without it the graph is uninterpretable — is the recall anchor here; watch for students who try to count symbols without consulting the key. The Math Talk on p.83 about 33 and 27 is a productive difficulty: let students struggle briefly before nudging them toward the idea of choosing a different scale.
materials: Coloured chalk or markers for drawing symbols

periods.activity_title: Constructing Pictographs: Choosing a Scale That Works

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Prepare a pictograph using one symbol = 100 kites for Magan Bhai's kite sales data (Chaman 250, Rani 300, Rukhsana 100, Jasmeet 450, Jetha Lal 250, Poonam Ben 700). Answer: (a) symbols for Rani; (b) maximum buyer; (c) Jasmeet vs Chaman; (d) whether Poonam Ben bought more than double Rani's amount.

time_bands.activity: Brief class review: teacher writes three data values on the board (100, 250, 450) and asks students to suggest a scale for a pictograph. Two or three students share their choices and explain why (divisibility, manageable symbol count). This surfaces scale-selection reasoning before the main task.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84 ("Prepare a pictograph using one symbol = 100 kites for Magan Bhai's kite sales data..."). They draw their pictograph in notebooks, then answer parts (a)–(d). Teacher circulates, checking that half-symbols are drawn for values of 250 and that Poonam Ben's row has seven full symbols.

Two volunteers display their pictographs on the board. Class compares: Are the keys stated? Are half-symbols used consistently? Does the pictograph allow quick comparison between buyers? Students offer one improvement each.

Teacher summarises the properties of pictographs established through the kite-sales task: visual and suggestive, quick for comparison, but limited when data values are not multiples of the chosen scale.

periods.teacher_notes: The kite-sales task is deliberately chosen to foreground the limitation of pictographs: values like 250 and 700 work with a scale of 100, but students often try a scale of 50 and end up with unwieldy symbol counts — letting them discover this and revise is more instructive than prescribing the scale first. Watch for students who draw partial symbols for 250 as one-quarter rather than one-half.

periods.activity_title: From Symbols to Bars: The Structure of a Bar Graph

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the bar graph of students absent per class (Classes I–VIII) to answer: In Class 2, how many were absent? Which class had maximum absences? Which class had full attendance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: Horizontal bar graph of vehicular traffic at a busy Delhi road crossing from 6 am to 12 noon (one unit = 100 vehicles). Demonstrates reading maximum (7–8 am, 1200 vehicles), minimum (6–7 am, ~150 vehicles), second highest, and computing combined intervals (8–10 am total ~1800 vehicles).

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws side by side on the board a simple pictograph (3 rows, symbol = 2) and a bar graph of the same data, then asks: 'What is different? What is the same?' Students identify that both show categories and frequencies, but bars use length rather than counted symbols, and precision is easier with bars.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86 ("Use the bar graph of students absent per class, Classes I–VIII..."), reading off bar heights and answering the three sub-questions. Teacher asks students to state which bar reaches the zero line to answer the full-attendance question.

Class works through Example, section 4.3 p.87 ("Horizontal bar graph of vehicular traffic at a busy Delhi road crossing from 6 am to 12 noon...") together. Teacher reads the axis labels aloud, students identify the scale (one unit = 100 vehicles), then answer: maximum bar, minimum bar, combined 8–10 am. The horizontal orientation is compared with the vertical bars seen in the absent-student graph.

Teacher names the three structural rules of bar graphs — uniform bar width, equal spacing, scale starting from zero — and asks a student to point to each feature in the Delhi traffic graph on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked with pictographs may assume a bar graph also needs a symbol key; clarify that the bar's height against the scale axis is the only reading tool needed. A common error when reading horizontal bar graphs is confusing the category axis (vertical, listing time intervals) with the value axis (horizontal, carrying the scale).

periods.activity_title: Reading Bar Graphs: Traffic, Population, and Reasoning from Data

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many total vehicles passed through the Delhi crossing between 6 am and noon?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think so little traffic occurred during 6–7 am compared to later hours?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think traffic was heaviest between 7–8 am?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think traffic was lesser and lesser each hour after 8 am until noon?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.89
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk on India population bar graph: (a) what questions might you ask friends based on the graph; (b) how much did population increase over 50 years and in each decade?

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 4.3 p.88 (total-vehicle count, and three reasoning questions about why traffic varies across time intervals). They first compute the total from the bar graph, then write one-sentence justifications for each reasoning question. Pairs compare their reasoning sentences.

Class discusses the three reasoning questions (Q2–Q4, p.88) as a whole group. Teacher writes student answers on the board and helps distinguish 'reading the bar' (a computational act) from 'explaining the pattern' (a reasoning act), showing that both are valid uses of a bar graph.

Students work on the Math Talk, section 4.3 p.89 ("India population bar graph...") — generating their own questions from the graph (sub-part a) and computing population increases per decade (sub-part b). Groups share the questions they posed.
Teacher notes that bar graphs allow both exact reading (scale + bar height) and qualitative reasoning (trends, comparisons); students name one fact and one trend they found in the population graph.

periods.teacher_notes: The reasoning questions E-17 to E-19 are genuinely open — multiple justifications are valid — so resist funnelling students to a single answer. For the India population graph, watch for students who compute decade-by-decade differences by subtracting bar heights visually rather than from the scale values; prompt them to read off the scale before subtracting.

periods.activity_title: Step by Step: Drawing a Bar Graph from a Frequency Table

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.4 p.90
textbook_items_in_class.description: Vertical bar graph of runs scored by Smriti in 8 cricket matches (scores: 80, 50, 10, 100, 90, 0, 90, 50). Demonstrates selecting scale of 1 unit = 10 runs to avoid impractically tall bars and drawing the completed bar graph.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use Imran's expenditure bar graph to answer: (1) which item family spends most and second most on; (2) is electricity cost about half the education cost; (3) is education cost less than one-fourth the food cost?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10, Beetles 5, Butterflies 3, Grasshoppers 2.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five-step bar-graph procedure on the board: (1) draw two perpendicular axes, (2) label categories on horizontal axis, (3) choose a scale, (4) compute bar heights from frequencies, (5) draw bars of uniform width. Then the class works through Example, section 4.4 p.90 ("Vertical bar graph of runs scored by Smriti in 8 cricket matches...") step by step, with students calling out each step number as the teacher draws.

Students read Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.93 ("Use Imran's expenditure bar graph to answer...") — three interpretation sub-questions — individually. Answers are taken orally: the teacher asks students to state the bar height and the scale calculation that produced each answer.

Students draw the bar graph for Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93 ("Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10...") in their notebooks, following the five-step procedure. Teacher circulates and checks that axes are labelled, scale is stated, and bar widths are uniform.
Quick check: teacher asks students to hold up their notebooks and scans for bars with unequal widths or missing scale labels — two common errors — before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Walked through as a deductive procedure, the five-step method gives students a replicable algorithm; watch for the tendency to omit the scale label on the vertical axis, which makes the graph unreadable. Example WE-4 (Example, section 4.4 p.91) on Imran's family expenditure is not walked through in class here — it is available as a self-study reference for students who want to see scale-by-division applied to larger values.

periods.activity_title: Scale Selection and Partially Drawn Graphs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pooja's partially erased bar graph of railway tickets sold for five MP cities (Vidisha 24, Jabalpur 20, Seoni 16, Indore 28, Sagar 16). Sub-parts: (a) tickets for Vidisha; (b) for Jabalpur; (c) determine the scale; (d) draw correct bar for Sagar; (e) add scale numbers to vertical axis; (f) are Seoni and Indore bars correct?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Chinu's transport data (bikes, cars, bicycles, autos, scooters, buses, bullock carts seen in one hour). Sub-parts: (a) prepare frequency distribution table; (b) most used transport; (c) describe process for collecting this data.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.93 ("Pooja's partially erased bar graph of railway tickets sold for five MP cities...") — all six sub-parts. Working backwards from a partially drawn graph to determine its scale (sub-part c) is the key challenge; teacher prompts students to look at a bar whose value they know and count the grid units it spans.

Class discussion of Q2: teacher draws the completed graph on the board collaboratively, with students directing each step. Sub-part (f) — checking whether Seoni and Indore bars are correct — is discussed last, connecting scale-determination back to bar-drawing accuracy.

Students begin Figure it Out Q3, section 4.4 p.94 ("Chinu's transport data...") — sub-parts (a) and (b): prepare a frequency distribution table from the given tally and identify the most-used transport. Sub-part (c), describing the data-collection process, is set as an oral exit task — one student shares their answer before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The reverse-engineering challenge of Q2 (deducing the scale from a partially drawn graph) is a strong problem-solving task; the most common stumbling block is students who try to guess the scale rather than calculating it from a known bar. Remind students that the scale must work for all bars, not just one.

periods.activity_title: Dice, Frequency Tables, and Drawing Your Own Bar Graph

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95
textbook_items_in_class.description: Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes, prepare frequency distribution table with tally marks. Find: (a) number appearing minimum times; (b) number appearing maximum times; (c) numbers appearing equal number of times.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95
textbook_items_in_class.description: Faiz's frequency table of Bumrah's wickets in 30 matches. Sub-parts: (a) what information does the table give; (b) possible title; (c) what catches attention; (d) matches with 4 wickets; (e) why Mayank's method of adding 0+1+2+...+7 is wrong; (f) correct method to find total wickets.

time_bands.activity: In pairs, students roll a die (or simulate rolling by writing outcomes drawn from a bag of numbered slips) 30 times, record outcomes using tally marks, complete the frequency table, and answer sub-parts (a)–(c) of Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95 ("Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes..."). Teacher notes whose tallies sum to exactly 30 — a quick integrity check.

Two pairs share their frequency tables. Class observes that different pairs get different frequencies; teacher asks: 'Is this surprising? Why might the frequencies not all be equal?' This surfaces an informal sense of randomness without naming it technically.

Students work on Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95 ("Faiz's frequency table of Bumrah's wickets in 30 matches..."). Sub-part (e) — why Mayank's method (adding 0+1+2+…+7) is wrong — is the conceptual focus; students write their explanation before hearing the class answer.

Teacher confirms the correct method for total wickets (frequency × wicket count for each row, then sum) and connects it to the original definition of frequency as a count, reinforcing that frequency and value are multiplied, not summed.

periods.teacher_notes: The die-rolling task gives a concrete, playful context for frequency tables — the key learning is that the same data-organisation procedure applies regardless of whether data comes from a classroom survey or a randomised experiment. The Mayank error in E-26 (adding category values instead of multiplying by frequency) is one of the most persistent conceptual errors in data handling; take extra time on sub-part (e).
materials: One die per pair (or numbered paper slips in a bag)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 4.4 p.96
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tractors pictograph for five villages. Answer: (a) village with fewest tractors; (b) most tractors; (c) how many more tractors Village C has than Village B; (d) is Komal correct that Village D has half the tractors of Village E?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 4.4 p.97
textbook_items_in_class.description: Girl students pictograph for Classes 1–8 (each symbol = 4 girls). Answer: (a) class with fewest girls; (b) difference between Classes 5 and 6; (c) how graph changes if 2 more girls join Class 2; (d) how many girls in Class 7.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 4.4 p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mudhol Hounds dog counts in six Karnataka villages (A:18, B:36, C:12, D:48, E:18, F:24). Prepare a pictograph and answer: (a) useful scale/key; (b) symbols for Village B; (c) is Kamini correct that Villages B and D together exceed the other four?

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q6, section 4.4 p.96 ("Tractors pictograph for five villages...") individually — all four sub-parts. The comparison question (how many more tractors in C than B) requires students to read both bars, apply the key, and subtract; teacher watches for students who subtract symbol counts rather than actual values.

Students work on Figure it Out Q7, section 4.4 p.97 ("Girl students pictograph for Classes 1–8, each symbol = 4 girls..."). Sub-part (c) — how the graph changes if two more girls join Class 2 — requires students to determine whether the additional girls complete a symbol or add a fraction; this surfaces the scale-and-remainder challenge.

Students work on Figure it Out Q8, section 4.4 p.98 ("Mudhol Hounds dog counts in six Karnataka villages...") — designing a pictograph from scratch. They first decide the scale (sub-part a), justify it, then draw the pictograph and verify Kamini's claim (sub-part c) by computing sums.
Quick class check: teacher asks 'What scale did you choose for the Mudhol Hounds graph and why?' Two students share different valid scales, reinforcing that scale choice is a design decision.

periods.teacher_notes: The Mudhol Hounds task (E-29) integrates both pictograph construction and arithmetic verification — Kamini's claim about Villages B and D requires actual computation, not just visual inspection. Watch for students who verify Kamini's claim by counting symbols instead of converting to actual dog counts using the key.

periods.activity_title: Bar Graphs from Survey Data and Error Detection

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: Survey of 120 students' preferred free-time activities (Playing 45, Reading 30, Watching TV 20, Listening to music 10, Painting 15). Draw a bar graph (1 unit = 5 students). Which activity is preferred most after playing?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 4.4 p.99
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bar graph of tree saplings planted each day of a week by a school. Answer: (a) total saplings on Wednesday and Thursday; (b) total for the whole week; (c) day with most and least saplings planted, and reasons for the variation.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 4.4 p.99
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shagufta and Divya's bar graph of tiger counts in India 2006–2022 (in 4-year intervals: 1400, 1700, 2200, 3000, 3700) contains mistakes. Identify and fix the errors in the bars.

time_bands.activity: Students draw the bar graph for Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98 ("Survey of 120 students' preferred free-time activities...") using scale 1 unit = 5 students. After drawing, they answer the question about the second most preferred activity. Teacher checks that bar heights for values like 45 (= 9 units) are calculated correctly.

Students answer Figure it Out Q10, section 4.4 p.99 ("Bar graph of tree saplings planted each day of a week...") — reading off combined values and offering reasons for variation across days. This is primarily a reading-and-reasoning task; students write one-sentence justifications for part (c).

Students work on Figure it Out Q11, section 4.4 p.99 ("Shagufta and Divya's bar graph of tiger counts...") — identifying and correcting errors in a completed bar graph. Students annotate directly on the textbook page or redraw corrected bars in their notebooks.

Teacher asks: 'What kind of error did you find in Q11?' Students name the error type (wrong bar height, wrong scale label, etc.) — reinforcing that checking a completed graph is as important as drawing one.

periods.teacher_notes: Error-detection tasks like Q11 build critical graph-reading skills that complement construction; watch for students who can draw a correct graph themselves but cannot spot an error in someone else's. For Q9, students sometimes compute bar heights by dividing the frequency by the scale incorrectly — remind them that if 1 unit = 5 students, then 45 students = 45 ÷ 5 = 9 units, so the bar reaches the 45 mark on the scale axis.

periods.activity_title: When Design Helps and When It Misleads

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: Would you use vertical or horizontal bars to represent heights of the tallest persons in each class in your school? Why?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: For a table of longest rivers on each continent, would you prefer vertical or horizontal bars? Why? Find the data, make the table and bar graph. Which continents have the longest rivers?

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws two versions of the same mountain data on the board: one as a vertical bar graph with rectangular bars, one as an infographic using triangles of varying widths. Class discusses: 'Do both graphs give the same information? What extra impression does the triangle version create?' This surfaces the core principle that visual choices can introduce unintended meaning.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.103 ("Would you use vertical or horizontal bars to represent heights of the tallest persons in each class?"). They write a one-sentence justification. Teacher collects two or three responses and writes them on the board — students evaluate which justification is most precise.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.5 p.103 ("For a table of longest rivers on each continent, would you prefer vertical or horizontal bars? Why?..."). They reason about orientation (horizontal suits length-parallel-to-ground intuition), then construct a bar graph from the data they find or from a teacher-provided table on the board.

Class summarises the two design principles: (1) bar orientation should match the real-world direction of what is being measured; (2) artistic embellishment must not encode extra dimensions (width, colour gradient) that the data does not support.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the structural rules of bar graphs — uniform width, equal spacing, scale from zero — this unit extends reasoning to the question of why those rules matter aesthetically and communicatively. Watch for students who argue purely from personal preference ('vertical looks nicer') rather than from the intuitive alignment of orientation with the real-world attribute being measured.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a rapid oral review across the whole chapter by posing five questions, one per section: (1) What is the difference between raw data and a frequency table? (2) What must every pictograph include? (3) What three structural rules define a bar graph? (4) What five steps produce a bar graph from a frequency table? (5) Why does bar orientation matter? Students call out answers; teacher writes key phrases on the board.

Groups of four receive a fresh problem: a small dataset of their own class's preferred mode of transport to school (teacher either surveys the class in real time using a quick show of hands, or uses a fixed invented dataset on the board). Groups (a) organise the data into a tally-frequency table, (b) choose between a pictograph and a bar graph and justify the choice in writing, (c) draw their chosen graph with a stated scale, and (d) write two observations from the graph.

Each group displays their graph on the board or holds it up. Class evaluates each display against the chapter's criteria: Is the scale stated? Are bars uniform? Does orientation suit the data? Does any design choice introduce misleading information? Groups give each other one specific improvement.

Teacher asks three synthesis questions for individual written reflection: (1) When would you choose a pictograph over a bar graph? (2) What makes a graph misleading? (3) Give one example from daily life where collecting and organising data would help you make a better decision. Students write answers in notebooks; teacher reads two aloud to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The synthesis task is designed to run entirely within this unit: data is collected or provided here, organised here, represented here, and critiqued here. Connecting the full data journey — from the tally marks introduced when defining frequency to the aesthetic cautions about infographics — surfaces the coherence of the chapter as a single idea. Watch for groups who draw a pictograph for a dataset whose values are not clean multiples of their chosen scale, and use that moment to revisit scale selection as a design decision.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes what 'data' means in mathematics?

options.label: A
options.text: A single number used in a calculation

options.label: B
options.text: A collection of facts, numbers, observations, or descriptions that convey information

options.label: C
options.text: A chart drawn to show how numbers compare

options.label: D
options.text: The largest value in a list of numbers

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A collection of facts, numbers, observations, or descriptions that convey information.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of data as stated in section 4.1.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates data with an individual numeric value, missing that data is always a collection.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses data (the raw information) with a graph (a representation of that information).
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates data with a derived summary statistic rather than with the underlying collection itself.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the opening paragraph of section 4.1 and find the sentence that defines data.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give two examples of data from daily life — one numerical and one descriptive.

items.prompt: In a pictograph where each full symbol represents 10 children and a half symbol represents 5 children, the row for 'Sometimes' shows 2 full symbols and 1 half symbol. How many children does this row represent?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 25. Two full symbols = 2 × 10 = 20 children; one half symbol = 5 children; total = 25.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of full symbols by the key value and add the half-symbol value.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted only the full symbols and ignored the half symbol.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student counted only the half symbol and one full symbol, perhaps misreading the row.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student counted three full symbols, treating the half symbol as a full one.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at Example, section 4.2 p.80 to see how full and half symbols are counted step by step.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state what would happen if the row showed 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol, and what class size would make that impossible with a key of 1 symbol = 10.

exercise.description: Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours. Students read the pictograph (each symbol = 10 children) to find: children who always slept ≥9 hours (50), sometimes (25), and never (40). items.prompt: Which of the following is a structural rule that every bar graph must follow?

options.label: A
options.text: All bars must be drawn in different colours

options.label: B
options.text: The scale on the value axis must start from zero

options.label: C
options.text: The tallest bar must always be drawn first

options.label: D
options.text: Each bar must be labelled with its exact frequency inside the bar

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The scale on the value axis must start from zero.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the key properties of bar graphs stated in section 4.3: uniform width, equal spacing, and scale starting from zero.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses an optional aesthetic choice with a structural requirement.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student invents an ordering rule not stated anywhere in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses an optional annotation with a rule — frequency labels inside bars are not required.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to find the list of bar-graph properties in section 4.3 and read them aloud.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in one sentence why a scale that does not start from zero would make a bar graph misleading.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86
exercise.description: Use the bar graph of students absent per class (Classes I–VIII) to answer: In Class 2, how many were absent? Which class had maximum absences? Which class had full attendance?

items.prompt: A student wants to display the heights of the five tallest mountains in Asia. She draws an infographic where each mountain is shown as a triangle, and she makes taller mountains wider as well so they look more impressive. Explain why this design choice could mislead a reader, and state what she should do instead to present the data accurately.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Making taller mountains wider implies that taller mountains are also broader, which is additional information the data does not provide. A reader may wrongly conclude that mountain width corresponds to some real measurement. She should draw bars of uniform width so that only the height (length) of each bar encodes a data value, keeping visual impression aligned with the actual data.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the principle from section 4.5 that artistic choices must not encode extra dimensions the data does not support.

inclusivity.support: Let the student talk through their thinking with a partner before writing, focusing on what a reader's eye is drawn to in a wider shape.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to suggest a second artistic choice — such as using a gradient of colours — and reason whether that choice would or would not mislead a reader.

items.prompt: A teacher asks 20 students to name their favourite fruit. The responses are: Mango, Apple, Mango, Banana, Mango, Apple, Guava, Mango, Apple, Banana, Mango, Guava, Apple, Mango, Banana, Apple, Mango, Guava, Apple, Mango. Organise this data into a tally-marks frequency table. Then state: (a) the most popular fruit, (b) the frequency of Banana, and (c) the number of students who chose either Apple or Guava.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Frequency table: Mango — tally IIIII III — frequency 8; Apple — tally IIIII I — frequency 6; Banana — tally III — frequency 3; Guava — tally III — frequency 3. (a) Most popular fruit: Mango (frequency 8). (b) Frequency of Banana: 3. (c) Apple or Guava: 6 + 3 = 9 students.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Go through the raw list item by item, add a tally mark for each occurrence, group tallies in fives, then read off frequencies to answer each sub-question.

inclusivity.support: Give the student a blank table with fruit names already filled in so they only need to add tally marks row by row.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to arrange the four fruits in descending order of frequency and state what scale they would use if drawing a bar graph of this data.

items.prompt: A student lists her classmates' shoe sizes in the order she collected them: 4, 6, 5, 4, 7, 5, 6, 4, 5, 6, 7, 4, 5, 5, 6. She then arranges the data in ascending order. State the ascending-order list, the largest shoe size, the smallest shoe size, and how many students wear size 5.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ascending order: 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7. Largest shoe size: 7. Smallest shoe size: 4. Number of students wearing size 5: 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange values from smallest to largest, then scan the ordered list to read off the extremes and count repeated values.

inclusivity.support: Let the student use tally marks first — one mark per shoe size — and then read the counts off the tally table before writing the ordered list.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to also state how many students wear a size larger than 5, and to explain in one sentence how ascending order made that question easier to answer.

exercise.description: Math Talk: Are there other ways to arrange the shoe-size data?

items.prompt: A shop sold the following number of notebooks in five days: Monday 150, Tuesday 200, Wednesday 50, Thursday 100, Friday 250. Prepare a pictograph using a scale where one symbol represents 50 notebooks. State: (a) how many symbols you draw for Tuesday, (b) which day has the most symbols, and (c) whether Friday's sales are more than double Monday's sales.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Tuesday: 200 ÷ 50 = 4 symbols. (b) Friday has the most symbols: 250 ÷ 50 = 5 symbols. (c) Monday: 150 ÷ 50 = 3 symbols; double Monday = 6 symbols; Friday has 5 symbols, which is less than 6, so Friday's sales are NOT more than double Monday's sales (250 < 300).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each frequency by the scale value to find symbol count, then compare Friday's value with double Monday's value arithmetically.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw the pictograph physically, counting out symbols row by row, before answering part (c) by counting symbols.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain what scale they would choose if one of the values were 175, and why 50 is no longer a convenient choice.

Answer: (a) symbols for Rani; (b) maximum buyer; (c) Jasmeet vs Chaman; (d) whether Poonam Ben bought more than double Rani's amount.

items.prompt: A bar graph shows the number of visitors to a park across four seasons. The scale is 1 unit = 20 visitors. The bar heights are: Summer 8 units, Monsoon 3 units, Autumn 5 units, Winter 11 units. (a) How many visitors came in Summer? (b) How many more visitors came in Winter than in Monsoon? (c) What is the total number of visitors across all four seasons?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Summer: 8 × 20 = 160 visitors. (b) Winter: 11 × 20 = 220; Monsoon: 3 × 20 = 60; difference = 220 − 60 = 160 more visitors. (c) Total units = 8 + 3 + 5 + 11 = 27; total visitors = 27 × 20 = 540.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each bar's unit height by the scale value to recover the frequency, then perform the required arithmetic operations.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first write out the frequency for each season separately before attempting the difference and total.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to determine what scale they would use if the maximum bar height should not exceed 10 units for the same data.

items.prompt: A frequency table shows the number of students who chose each colour as their favourite: Red 15, Blue 25, Green 10, Yellow 20, Purple 5. Choose a suitable scale and state it. Then compute the bar height (in units) for each colour. Which colour has the tallest bar?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A suitable scale is 1 unit = 5 students (the maximum value 25 gives a bar of 5 units, which is manageable). Bar heights: Red = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 units; Blue = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 units; Green = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 units; Yellow = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 units; Purple = 5 ÷ 5 = 1 unit. Blue has the tallest bar.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a scale that divides all frequencies evenly and keeps bar heights practical, then divide each frequency by the scale to find bar height.

inclusivity.support: Provide the student with the scale (1 unit = 5 students) and ask them only to compute the bar heights.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to re-compute bar heights using a scale of 1 unit = 1 student and explain why that scale is impractical for drawing.

items.prompt: Samira's frequency table shows insects found in a garden: Ants 30, Beetles 10, Butterflies 5, Dragonflies 15, Grasshoppers 20. She uses a scale of 1 unit = 5 insects and draws the bar graph. (a) What is the bar height for Ants? (b) What is the bar height for Grasshoppers? (c) How many more units tall is the Ants bar than the Dragonflies bar?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Ants: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 units. (b) Grasshoppers: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 units. (c) Dragonflies: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 units; Ants bar − Dragonflies bar = 6 − 3 = 3 units more.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each frequency by the scale value to find bar height, then subtract to find the difference.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write the division sentence for each insect (e.g., 30 ÷ 5 = ?) before identifying bar heights.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state which insect has a bar exactly half as tall as the Ants bar, and verify by calculation.

exercise.description: Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10, Beetles 5, Butterflies 3, Grasshoppers 2.

items.prompt: A partially drawn bar graph shows railway tickets sold for three cities: City P bar reaches the 6-unit mark, City Q bar reaches the 4-unit mark. The frequency table says City P sold 24 tickets and City Q sold 16 tickets. (a) What is the scale of this bar graph? (b) City R sold 20 tickets. How many units tall should the bar for City R be?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) City P: 24 tickets, bar = 6 units; scale = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 tickets per unit. Check with City Q: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 units — but City Q bar is shown as 4 units, consistent. Scale = 1 unit = 4 tickets. (b) City R: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide a known frequency by its bar height to determine the scale, then apply that scale to the new frequency.

inclusivity.support: Tell the student to try City Q first: 16 tickets and 4 units — what does one unit equal? Then verify with City P.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state whether a scale of 1 unit = 2 tickets would also produce whole-number bar heights for all three cities, and which scale produces a more practical graph.

Sub-parts: (a) tickets for Vidisha; (b) for Jabalpur; (c) determine the scale; (d) draw correct bar for Sagar; (e) add scale numbers to vertical axis; (f) are Seoni and Indore bars correct?

items.prompt: In a dice-rolling experiment, a student rolled a die 30 times and recorded the following frequencies: 1 appeared 4 times, 2 appeared 7 times, 3 appeared 5 times, 4 appeared 6 times, 5 appeared 4 times, 6 appeared 4 times. (a) Verify that the total number of rolls is 30. (b) Which number appeared the maximum number of times? (c) Which numbers appeared the same number of times?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 4 + 7 + 5 + 6 + 4 + 4 = 30. Total confirmed. (b) The number 2 appeared the maximum number of times (7 times). (c) The numbers 1, 5, and 6 each appeared 4 times — they appeared the same number of times.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sum all frequencies to verify the total, then compare frequency values to find the maximum and identify ties.

inclusivity.support: Let the student add the frequencies in two groups of three to make the sum easier to manage.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state what bar heights they would use for each outcome if they drew a bar graph with a scale of 1 unit = 1 roll, and whether they would choose a different scale and why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95
exercise.description: Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes, prepare frequency distribution table with tally marks. Find: (a) number appearing minimum times; (b) number appearing maximum times; (c) numbers appearing equal number of times.

items.prompt: A cricket player's wicket frequency table for 20 matches shows: 0 wickets in 4 matches, 1 wicket in 6 matches, 2 wickets in 5 matches, 3 wickets in 3 matches, 4 wickets in 2 matches. A student says the total wickets taken is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Explain why this is wrong and compute the correct total number of wickets.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student added the wicket values (0, 1, 2, 3, 4) without accounting for how many times each occurred. The correct method is to multiply each wicket value by its frequency and sum the products: (0 × 4) + (1 × 6) + (2 × 5) + (3 × 3) + (4 × 2) = 0 + 6 + 10 + 9 + 8 = 33 wickets in total.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each category value by its frequency and sum all products to find the total.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write a separate multiplication for each row (e.g., 1 wicket × 6 matches = 6 wickets) before adding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to also compute the average wickets per match (33 ÷ 20) and state whether the player took more or fewer than 2 wickets per match on average.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95
exercise.description: Faiz's frequency table of Bumrah's wickets in 30 matches. Sub-parts: (a) what information does the table give; (b) possible title; (c) what catches attention; (d) matches with 4 wickets; (e) why Mayank's method of adding 0+1+2+...+7 is wrong; (f) correct method to find total wickets.

items.prompt: A pictograph shows the number of tractors in four villages. The key states: 1 symbol = 6 tractors. Village P has 3 symbols, Village Q has 5 symbols, Village R has 2 symbols, Village S has 4 symbols. (a) How many tractors does Village Q have? (b) How many more tractors does Village S have than Village R? (c) Do Villages P and R together have more tractors than Village Q alone?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Village Q: 5 × 6 = 30 tractors. (b) Village S: 4 × 6 = 24; Village R: 2 × 6 = 12; difference = 24 − 12 = 12 more tractors. (c) Village P: 3 × 6 = 18; Village R: 12; P + R = 18 + 12 = 30; Village Q = 30; they are equal, so P and R together do NOT have MORE tractors than Q — they have the same number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each village's symbol count by the key value to find actual tractor counts, then perform the required comparisons.

inclusivity.support: Let the student complete a small table with one column for symbol count and one for actual count before answering the questions.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state what scale they would choose if they wanted to represent all four villages in a bar graph where no bar exceeds 10 units.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 4.4 p.96
exercise.description: Tractors pictograph for five villages. Answer: (a) village with fewest tractors; (b) most tractors; (c) how many more tractors Village C has than Village B; (d) is Komal correct that Village D has half the tractors of Village E?

items.prompt: A pictograph of girl students uses a scale of 1 symbol = 4 girls. Class A has 2 symbols, Class B has 3 and a half symbols, Class C has 1 symbol. (a) How many girls are in Class B? (b) If 4 more girls join Class A, how many full symbols and half symbols will Class A now need? (c) Which class has the fewest girls?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Class B: 3 full symbols = 12 girls; half symbol = 2 girls; total = 14 girls. (b) Class A originally: 2 × 4 = 8 girls; after 4 more join: 8 + 4 = 12 girls; 12 ÷ 4 = 3 full symbols, 0 half symbols. (c) Class C: 1 × 4 = 4 girls — fewest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply symbol count by key value (and add half-symbol value where applicable) to find girl counts, then compare.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that a half symbol represents half of the key value — half of 4 is 2 — before attempting part (a).
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state what would happen to Class B's row if 2 more girls joined — would another half symbol or full symbol be needed, and why?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 4.4 p.97
exercise.description: Girl students pictograph for Classes 1–8 (each symbol = 4 girls). Answer: (a) class with fewest girls; (b) difference between Classes 5 and 6; (c) how graph changes if 2 more girls join Class 2; (d) how many girls in Class 7.

items.prompt: Dog counts in five villages are: Village A 24, Village B 36, Village C 12, Village D 48, Village E 24. You decide to draw a pictograph with a scale of 1 symbol = 12 dogs. (a) How many symbols does Village D need? (b) Verify whether Villages A and C together have as many dogs as Village B. (c) Does Village D have more than double the dogs of Village A?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Village D: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 symbols. (b) Village A: 24; Village C: 12; A + C = 36 = Village B (36). Yes, they are equal. (c) Double Village A = 2 × 24 = 48 = Village D. Village D has exactly double Village A's dogs, not more than double.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each village's count by the scale to find symbol count, then use actual dog counts for arithmetic comparisons.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first convert all five village counts to symbol counts, then re-read the actual values from that table for parts (b) and (c).
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain what scale they would use if one village had 18 dogs and why a scale of 12 would cause a problem.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 4.4 p.98
exercise.description: Mudhol Hounds dog counts in six Karnataka villages (A:18, B:36, C:12, D:48, E:18, F:24). Prepare a pictograph and answer: (a) useful scale/key; (b) symbols for Village B; (c) is Kamini correct that Villages B and D together exceed the other four?

items.prompt: A survey of 100 students found these preferred after-school activities: Sports 40, Reading 25, Drawing 15, Music 10, Cooking 10. Using a scale of 1 unit = 5 students, compute the bar height for each activity. Which activity is preferred second most after Sports?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Bar heights: Sports = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 units; Reading = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 units; Drawing = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 units; Music = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 units; Cooking = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 units. The second most preferred activity is Reading (frequency 25, bar height 5 units).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each frequency by the scale value to find bar heights, then rank to identify the second highest.

inclusivity.support: Provide a blank table with activity names and the division sentence (e.g., 40 ÷ 5 = ?) already written, so the student fills in the answers.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to check whether Music and Cooking having the same frequency means their bars would look the same, and what that implies for reading the graph.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98
exercise.description: Survey of 120 students' preferred free-time activities (Playing 45, Reading 30, Watching TV 20, Listening to music 10, Painting 15). Draw a bar graph (1 unit = 5 students). Which activity is preferred most after playing?
